title: The plate of three things
hookLine: on this plate are three things, truth, contentment and reflection, the seal on the Granth (Mundavani, ang 1429)
tomorrow: The Lord stood to finish the work

lines: A STEEL PLATE ON A CLOTH.
cards: A steel plate, a thaal, set down on a cloth. In a Sikh home or a gurdwara you might see one holding karah prashad, or food for a guest.
Now turn to Ang fourteen hundred twenty-nine, near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Guru Arjan sets down a plate of his own and tells you exactly what's on it. Not sweets, not bread.
Three things, and then a fourth that holds the others up. It's the Mundavani, and it comes near the close of the Granth like a seal on a letter.

teach.b: You met this plate before, at the Granth's four-hundredth year; today, a closer look. Here it is, paraphrased. On this plate, three things have been placed: truth, contentment and reflection.
The nectar of the Lord's Name has been placed here too, the support of all. Whoever eats it, whoever enjoys it, is saved. This can't be given up; keep it always in your heart.
The dark world-ocean is crossed by holding to the Lord's feet; Nanak, all of this is the Lord's own spreading out.
Mundavani is often explained as a seal, the kind pressed into wax to close a letter. So near its close, the Granth names what was inside it all along. Take the three one at a time.
Sat, truth: not only telling the truth, but living close to what's real.
Santokh, contentment: enough, the end of the endless more. Vichar, reflection: turning the teaching over in the mind. Then the Name, amrit naam, laid beside them as the thing everything rests on.

teach.h: EAT IT, KEEP IT IN YOUR HEART.
teach.b: Notice the verbs: eat, enjoy, keep it in your heart. This plate isn't for a shelf. It's a meal.

Sikhs read the Mundavani at the completion of a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, so a long reading ends at a table: truth to stand on, enough to rest in, reflection to grow by, and the Name to feed them.

how: Sikhs read the Mundavani as part of the bhog, the completion of a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and its opening line about the plate of three things is often explained in katha.

o: the ring a Sikh bride and groom exchange
a sweet offering handed out at the end of worship
the seal: a plate of truth, contentment and reflection

games.q: what's on the plate: tap the pairs.

s: the Mundavani's plate is only to be admired
the verbs are eat, enjoy, keep it in your heart: it's a meal.
the Lord's Name is placed on the plate beside the three things
the nectar of the Name is laid there too, the support of all.
the Mundavani sits near the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib
it's on Ang 1429, near the end, like a seal on a letter.

games.q: you've reached the end of a long reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. the seal sets down a plate. what's on it?
o: truth, contentment and reflection, with the Lord's Name.
nothing; the plate is empty on purpose.
games.why: three things and the nectar of the Name, the support of all, and the Guru says to eat it and keep it in your heart.

practice: Set out any plate and three small things nearby, a coin, a key, a leaf, and lay them down one at a time, naming each: truth, contentment, reflection.
Then sit with the plate in front of you and ask quietly which of the three your day needs most, without trying to solve anything. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you look.

wordCard.voice: Mundavani. The seal: Guru Arjan's plate of truth, contentment and reflection, with the Lord's Name, near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's word.

orig.note: the seal: Guru Arjan's closing composition on Ang 1429.

carryVoice: Your line: truth, contentment, reflection. The Name sits on the plate beside them. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Mundavani Mahala 5, Ang 1429 (thaal vich tinn vastu paio, sat santokh vicharo)
